Rifa'a's irrevocably divorced wife, describing her new husband by her veil's fringe, is told she cannot return to Rifa'a until Abdur-Rahman consummates their marriage.
The Prophet put on his Rida and walked, Zaid and Ali following, to the house where Hamza was, and asked permission to enter.
Asked what a Muhrim wears, the Prophet said no shirt, trousers, hooded cloak or Khuffs, unless he lacks sandals, when he cuts the Khuffs below the ankles.
The Prophet clothed the dead Abdullah bin Ubai in his own shirt and moved to offer his funeral prayer; Umar objected, and a verse then forbade praying over hypocrites.
The Prophet likened the charitable man and the miser to two men in iron cloaks, one widening as he gives and one tightening, showing it at his own shirt's opening.
On a journey the Prophet made ablution in a narrow-sleeved cloak, drawing his arms out from beneath it, and wiped over his Khuffs, worn after ablution.
The Prophet kept a Qaba for Makhrama and took off a silk Farruj after praying in it as unfit for the God-fearing; Anas wore a yellow hooded cloak of Khazz.
A Muhrim does not wear shirts, turbans, trousers, hooded cloaks, clothes touched by saffron or Wars, or Khuffs; lacking sandals he cuts Khuffs short, lacking an Izar he wears trousers.
Allowed to leave Mecca, the Prophet came to Abu Bakr at midday, head covered; Asma tied their food bag with her girdle, and they stayed three nights in Thour's cave.
The Prophet entered Mecca in a helmet, smiled and gave to a bedouin who yanked his Burd, and gave a woman's Burda to a man wanting it as his shroud.
Seventy thousand of the Prophet's followers will enter Paradise without accounts, faces shining like the moon; Ukasha, lifting his sheet, asked to be among them and was prayed for.
Hibra, a Yemeni cloth, was the garment the Prophet loved most, and when he died he was covered with a Hibra Burd.
When his illness worsened the Prophet, covering his face with a Khamisa, cursed the Jews and Christians for taking their prophets' graves as places of worship, warning his followers.
The Prophet sent a patterned Khamisa that distracted him in prayer to Abu Jahm for a plain sheet, and Aisha showed the Kisa and Izar he died wearing.
The Prophet forbade one-garment wraps baring a side or the private parts, and Mulamasa and Munabadha sales; he dressed little Um Khalid in a black Khamisa, wishing her long life.
Rifa'a's divorced wife, her skin bruised green, calls Abdur-Rahman impotent; he denies it, and the Prophet says she cannot return to Rifa'a without consummation, noting the sons resembling him.
On the day of Uhud Sa'd saw two men in white clothes at the Prophet's right and left whom he never saw before or after.
Whoever says none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and dies believing it enters Paradise, even with illegal sexual intercourse and theft, the Prophet repeated to Abu Dharr.
Silk is forbidden beyond two fingers' width; who wears it here will not hereafter; itch excused Az-Zubair and Abdur-Rahman; Ali's silk went to his wives, Umar's to sell or give.
Umar names Aisha and Hafsa as the two wives who backed each other against the Prophet, telling of his warnings and the Prophet's twenty-nine days in his upper room.
One night the Prophet woke exclaiming at afflictions and treasures sent down, asked who would wake the rooms' women, and said many well dressed here will be naked at Resurrection.
The Prophet dressed Um Khalid in a Khamisa, forbade men saffron, wore a red suit, and prayed in shoes; put the right shoe on first, and never walk in one.
People sought the Prophet's leftover ablution water at his red leather tent; he prayed at night within a mat screen, urging steady deeds, and kept a gold-buttoned cloak for Makhrama.
The Prophet forbade gold rings; he threw away the gold ring he had made, saying he would never wear it, and wore a silver ring, its stone silver too.
The Prophet married a woman who offered herself to a man who could not find even an iron ring as Mahr, for the Quran he knew by heart.
A silver ring the Prophet had engraved 'Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah' sealed his letters, and Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman wore it until it fell into Aris well.
After the Eid prayer, offered before the sermon, the Prophet went to the women and told them to give alms, and they put their rings in Bilal's garment.
On Eid the Prophet prayed two rak'at with no prayer before or after, then went to the women and ordered alms, and they gave their earrings and necklaces.
When a necklace Aisha had borrowed from Asma was lost, the men searching for it prayed without ablution for lack of water, and Allah revealed the verse of Tayammum.
On Eid day the Prophet prayed two rak'at with no optional prayer before or after, then went with Bilal to the women and ordered alms, and they gave their earrings.
In a Medina market the Prophet called for little Al-Hasan, who came wearing a bead necklace; he embraced him and asked Allah to love him and those who love him.
The Prophet cursed men who take on women's manners and women who take on men's, had such people turned out of houses, and barred an effeminate man from his wives.
The Fitra's practices are circumcision, shaving pubic hair, clipping nails, removing armpit hair and cutting moustaches short, while the beard is kept, unlike the pagans.
The Prophet had too few grey hairs to dye; Um Salama kept some of his reddish dyed hair; Jews and Christians do not dye, so do otherwise.
Handsome in a red cloak, the Prophet was neither tall nor short, his hair neither curly nor straight; sent at forty, he died at sixty with barely ten white hairs.
In a dream near the Ka'ba the Prophet saw the Messiah son of Mary, his combed hair dripping, circling it, then the curly-haired Dajjal, blind in the right eye.
The Prophet's wavy hair hung to his shoulders or just above, and he had big hands and feet, soft palms and a good-looking face, unlike anyone else.
Ibn Abbas had not heard the Prophet say 'Kafir' is written between the Dajjal's eyes, but heard him liken Abraham to himself and describe brown, curly-haired Moses saying Labbaik.
Umar said whoever braids his hair should shave it on leaving Ihram; the Prophet, his hair gummed, said the Talbiya, and having garlanded his Hadi kept Ihram until slaughtering it.
The Prophet first let his hair hang down like the people of the Scripture, not parted like the pagans', then parted it; Aisha recalled its parting shining in Ihram.
